disclaimer: Reference fixture in the simulator trace schema (v2). The scenarios are written by hand, but every function, theorem, predicate, right and error they name is the kernel's own: the sync resolves each declaration in the pinned seLe4n checkout and fails if one is missing. The kernel does not yet export JSON traces; when it does (source == "kernel"), steps become a replay of a real run.

propertyCatalog.label: No capability, no access
propertyCatalog.statement: A syscall reaches its operation only after the caller's CSpace resolves the named slot to a capability carrying the right that syscall requires; the lookup itself changes no state.

propertyCatalog.label: Derived authority never grows
propertyCatalog.statement: A minted capability names the same object as its parent and carries a subset of the parent's rights.

propertyCatalog.label: A refused syscall changes nothing
propertyCatalog.statement: A kernel transition has type SystemState → Except KernelError (α × SystemState): an error carries no successor state, so every refusal leaves the system exactly as it was.
propertyCatalog.caveat: This holds by the type of a transition rather than by a separate theorem.

propertyCatalog.label: Non-interference
propertyCatalog.statement: Every NonInterferenceStep, and every trace of them, preserves low-equivalence: what an observer at one security level can see does not depend on higher-level state.
propertyCatalog.caveat: Stated over the NonInterferenceStep relation (35 constructors). The theorem over the live checked syscall entry holds given a per-arm hypothesis.

propertyCatalog.label: IPC never flows down the lattice
propertyCatalog.statement: The endpoint flow gate admits a message only if the global security lattice allows the flow from sender to receiver; an endpoint override can narrow that, never widen it.

propertyCatalog.label: Memory isolation
propertyCatalog.statement: Carving from untyped memory preserves the untyped-memory invariant: watermarks stay inside their regions and carved children never overlap. Distinct address-space roots carry distinct ASIDs.

propertyCatalog.label: W^X: no page is writable and executable
propertyCatalog.statement: Any successful vspaceMapPage was given W^X-compliant permissions; the syscall decoder already refuses a write+execute request before any lookup.

propertyCatalog.label: Invariant preservation
propertyCatalog.statement: The syscall entry preserves proofLayerInvariantBundle, the 16-conjunct composition of every subsystem invariant.
propertyCatalog.caveat: Compositional: the theorem takes, as a hypothesis, that the dispatched operation preserves the bundle, and per-operation preservation theorems discharge it arm by arm.

propertyCatalog.label: Scheduling discipline
propertyCatalog.statement: The per-core selector picks the best thread of the highest-priority bucket (priority, then earliest deadline, then FIFO), and a scheduling context can never consume more than 8 × its budget.
propertyCatalog.caveat: Optimality is stated over the maximum-priority bucket, not the whole queue; the CBS bound is the static 8 × budget ceiling. There is no unconditional no-starvation theorem.

invariantCatalog.label: Endpoint queues well-formed
invariantCatalog.meaning: Every endpoint's send and receive queues are well-formed intrusive lists whose members are blocked on that endpoint.

invariantCatalog.label: No thread queued twice
invariantCatalog.meaning: No thread appears twice in an endpoint queue.

invariantCatalog.label: Blocked threads are not runnable
invariantCatalog.meaning: A thread blocked on send, receive, reply or a notification is never in a run queue.

invariantCatalog.label: Notification waiters consistent
invariantCatalog.meaning: A notification's waiter list holds exactly the threads blocked on it.

invariantCatalog.label: Running thread is not queued
invariantCatalog.meaning: The thread a core is running is not also in its run queue.

invariantCatalog.label: Current thread is a TCB
invariantCatalog.meaning: Whatever a core records as its current thread is a thread control block in the object store.

invariantCatalog.label: Budget within bounds
invariantCatalog.meaning: A scheduling context's remaining budget never exceeds its configured budget.

invariantCatalog.label: Derivation tree consistent
invariantCatalog.meaning: The capability derivation tree's parent and child maps agree with each other and with the slots they name.

invariantCatalog.label: Derivation tree acyclic
invariantCatalog.meaning: No capability is derived, directly or transitively, from itself.

invariantCatalog.label: Untyped watermark in bounds
invariantCatalog.meaning: Each untyped's allocation watermark stays inside its region.

invariantCatalog.label: Carved objects never overlap
invariantCatalog.meaning: The children carved from one untyped occupy disjoint memory.

invariantCatalog.label: No writable+executable page
invariantCatalog.meaning: No mapping in any address space is both writable and executable.

invariantCatalog.label: ASIDs unique
invariantCatalog.meaning: Each ASID names at most one address-space root.

invariantCatalog.label: No stale TLB entries
invariantCatalog.meaning: Every cached translation corresponds to a live mapping; an unmap shoots the entry down.

invariantCatalog.label: Audit log bounded
invariantCatalog.meaning: The declassification audit log never exceeds its capacity; a full log refuses the downgrade.

scenarios.title: IPC call and reply
scenarios.summary: A client calls a server through an endpoint capability. The checked entry resolves the capability and its write right, the message rendezvouses with the waiting server, the client blocks for the reply, and the reply wakes it.

steps.title: Initial state
steps.narrative: The client is running. The server has already called receive on the service endpoint, so it sits blocked on the endpoint's receive queue; only the idle thread is runnable.

steps.title: client → call(service-ep)

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: The capability gate resolves the client's slot to the endpoint capability and checks the write right a call requires. The flow gate admits the message (both threads share a domain). A receiver is waiting, so the kernel pops it from the receive queue, copies the two message registers, makes the server runnable, and blocks the client on the reply.

steps.title: schedule → server
steps.narrative: The running thread has blocked, so the core reschedules. The per-core selector takes the best thread of the highest-priority bucket: the server (180) beats idle (0). The kernel switches to it.

steps.title: server → reply(client)

syscall.capPath: server CSpace → reply capability for client

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: The server replies through the reply capability the call created. The kernel checks that the client is blocked on a reply from this server, copies the answer, and makes the client runnable again.

steps.title: server → receive(service-ep)

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: The server loops back for the next request. No sender is queued, so it blocks on the endpoint's receive queue and leaves the runnable set.

steps.title: schedule → client
steps.narrative: The server has blocked, so the core reschedules and switches to the client (200), which finds the reply in its message registers.

scenarios.title: The capability gate refuses
scenarios.summary: An application holds only a read capability to a service endpoint. Sending needs the write right, so the gate refuses before any operation runs; naming an empty slot is refused too. Each refusal leaves the state untouched. Receiving, which needs read, goes through.

steps.title: Initial state
steps.narrative: The app's CSpace holds one capability to the service endpoint, minted with the read right only. Slot 5 of its CSpace is empty.

steps.title: app → send(service-ep) — refused

syscall.capPath: app CSpace slot 4 → service-ep capability (rights: r)

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: The slot resolves to a real endpoint capability, but send requires the write right and this capability carries only read. syscallLookupCap returns .illegalAuthority, so the send operation is never invoked and no state changes.

steps.title: app → call(slot 5) — refused

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: Slot 5 holds no capability, so resolution fails before any right is examined. Authority cannot be guessed or forged: an address that names nothing is a refusal, not a default.

steps.title: app → receive(service-ep)

syscall.capPath: app CSpace slot 4 → service-ep capability (rights: r)

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: Receive requires only read, which this capability carries, so the gate admits it. No sender is waiting, so the app blocks on the receive queue and the core falls back to idle.

scenarios.title: Notification signal and wait
scenarios.summary: A driver signals a notification a handler is waiting on: the handler becomes runnable, without preempting the driver. A second signal finds no waiter, so its badge is OR-ed into the pending word, and the handler's next wait consumes it without blocking.

steps.title: Initial state
steps.narrative: The handler has called wait on the alarm notification and is blocked on it. The driver is running.

steps.title: driver → signal(alarm, badge 1)

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: A waiter is present, so the kernel dequeues it, delivers the badge in its message, and makes it runnable. Signal does not preempt: the driver keeps the core even though the handler has the higher priority, until the driver next yields or is rescheduled.

steps.title: driver → signal(alarm, badge 4)

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: Nobody is waiting now, so nothing is woken: the notification becomes active and the badge is OR-ed into its pending word. Signals accumulate rather than queue.

steps.title: schedule → handler
steps.narrative: At the driver's next scheduling point the selector compares the runnable threads; the handler (200) outranks the driver (150), which goes back to the run queue.

steps.title: handler → wait(alarm)

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: A badge is pending, so the wait consumes it immediately: the handler receives badge 4, the notification returns to idle, and the handler does not block.

scenarios.title: Budget exhaustion and EDF tie-break
scenarios.summary: A timer tick exhausts the running thread's scheduling-context budget. The kernel charges it, schedules a replenishment, moves its CBS deadline and re-queues it; the selector then breaks the priority tie by earliest deadline.

steps.title: Initial state
steps.narrative: Alpha is running with one tick of budget left. Beta has the same priority (180) and an earlier deadline; gamma has the earliest deadline of all but a lower priority.

steps.title: timer tick — alpha's budget exhausted
steps.narrative: The tick charges alpha's scheduling context. Its last unit is consumed, so the kernel schedules a replenishment one period later, moves the CBS deadline forward, and re-inserts alpha into the run queue as preempted.

steps.title: select beta: same priority, earlier deadline
steps.narrative: The selector considers only the highest-priority bucket, 180: alpha and beta. Gamma's earlier deadline does not matter, because priority is compared first. Between equals the earlier deadline wins, so beta (20) beats alpha (70).

steps.title: timer tick — beta charged
steps.narrative: The next tick charges one unit of beta's budget. Budget remains, so beta keeps the core.

scenarios.title: Minting, attenuation and revocation
scenarios.summary: A supervisor mints attenuated capabilities from a master endpoint capability. Asking for more rights than the parent holds is refused. Deleting a capability that has derivations is refused too; revocation removes exactly the derived capabilities and leaves the source in place.

steps.title: Initial state
steps.narrative: The supervisor holds the master capability to the service endpoint, with read, write and grant.

steps.title: supervisor → cspaceMint(app, w, badge 7)

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: Minting needs the grant right on the source. The requested rights {w} are a subset of the master's {r, w, g}, so the kernel inserts a badged child capability in the app's CSpace and records a mint edge in the derivation tree.

steps.title: supervisor → cspaceMint(app → rwg) — refused

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: Using the app's capability as the source fails at the gate: it carries only w, and minting needs grant. Even with grant, a request for rights the parent lacks would be refused inside the mint with .invalidCapability. Either way nothing is written.

steps.title: supervisor → cspaceCopy(app → app′)

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: A copy duplicates a capability unchanged and also needs grant. The copy becomes a child of the app capability in the derivation tree.

steps.title: supervisor → cspaceMint(logger, r, badge 9)

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: A second, read-only child for the logger, with its own badge so the server can tell the two clients apart.

steps.title: supervisor → cspaceDelete(app) — refused

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: The app capability still has a derivation (app′). Deleting it would orphan that child, so the delete refuses with .revocationRequired: derived authority has to be revoked first, never silently left behind.

steps.title: supervisor → cspaceRevoke(app)

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: Revocation is authorised by write on the slot it starts from. It destroys exactly the capabilities derived from app (here app′) and leaves app itself, and its siblings, in place.

scenarios.title: Carving and resetting untyped memory
scenarios.summary: Every object's memory is carved from an untyped region by untypedRetype, which advances a watermark. A carve that does not fit is refused. Resetting the untyped is refused while any capability still names a carved object; once those are revoked, the reset hands the whole region back.

steps.title: Initial state
steps.narrative: The supervisor holds a capability, with the retype right, to a 16 KiB RAM untyped. Nothing has been carved yet.

steps.title: supervisor → untypedRetype(frame, 4 KiB)

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: The carve checks, in order, that the untyped exists, that the child id is fresh, that the size is large enough and aligned, and that the region has room. A 4 KiB frame fits, so the watermark advances and a frame capability is placed in slot 8.

steps.title: supervisor → untypedRetype(untyped, 8 KiB)

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: A carve makes either a frame or a child untyped. This one carves an 8 KiB child untyped, which can be carved further and is retired with its parent.

steps.title: supervisor → untypedRetype(frame, 8 KiB) — refused

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: Only 4 KiB remain below the region's end, so the allocation fails with .untypedRegionExhausted. The watermark cannot pass the region boundary, and nothing is carved.

steps.title: supervisor → untypedReset — refused

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: The frame and the child untyped are still named by capabilities. Handing their memory back now would leave those capabilities pointing at reusable memory, so the reset refuses with .revocationRequired.

steps.title: supervisor → cspaceRevoke(untyped)

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: Revoking the untyped capability destroys every capability derived from it, the frame's and the child untyped's. The objects still occupy the region, but nothing can reach them any more.

steps.title: supervisor → untypedReset

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: Now nothing references the carved subtree, so the reset retires it, unmapping any page of the region first, and rewinds the watermark: the memory can be carved again.

scenarios.title: Information flow and declassification
scenarios.summary: Three security domains ordered public ⊑ app ⊑ secret. A secret thread's message to a public endpoint is refused at the flow gate; a public thread's message up to a secret endpoint is allowed. Declassification does not open a path: it records an authorised downgrade in the audit log.

steps.title: Initial state
steps.narrative: Each thread and endpoint carries a security label. Information may flow up the lattice (public → app → secret), never down. The secret worker is running.

steps.title: sec-worker → send(public-ep) — refused

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: The worker holds a valid write capability, so the capability gate passes. The flow gate then asks whether secret may flow to public; securityFlowsTo says no, so the send is refused with .flowDenied. Holding a capability is necessary, never sufficient, to move information.

steps.title: schedule → pub-client
steps.narrative: The worker yields; the public client runs.

steps.title: pub-client → send(secret-ep)

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: Public may flow up to secret, so the gate admits the message and it is delivered to the waiting secret server. Nothing about the secret side can flow back through this step.

steps.title: schedule → sec-server
steps.narrative: The secret server (180) outranks the public client and runs.

steps.title: sec-server → declassify(public object)

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: Neither domain comes from the caller: the source is the running thread's domain and the destination is the target object's. The declassification policy authorises secret → public for this actor, so the kernel appends one entry to the audit log. That is its only write: no object and no policy edge changes, so secret → public is still refused for ordinary IPC.

scenarios.title: Mapping pages under W^X
scenarios.summary: A loader maps frames into an address space through frame capabilities. Read-execute code and read-write data map; a write-and-execute request is refused by the argument decoder before any lookup. Unmapping shoots the cached translation down.

steps.title: Initial state
steps.narrative: The loader holds a capability to the app's address space (ASID 1) and capabilities to two frames carved earlier.

steps.title: loader → vspaceMap(code frame, r-x)

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: The decoder accepts r-x. The map takes its physical page from a frame capability, never from a raw address, and checks the frame may be mapped this way; the page-table write then checks W^X again and the translation is cached.

steps.title: loader → vspaceMap(data frame, rw-)

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: Writable data is mapped non-executable. A writable mapping also needs the write right on the frame capability itself.

steps.title: loader → vspaceMap(rwx) — refused

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: Write together with execute is not a permission value the decoder will construct: PagePermissions.ofNat? rejects it, so the syscall fails with .invalidSyscallArgument before any capability is looked up. The page-table layer would refuse it as well (.policyDenied); the decoder simply gets there first.

steps.title: loader → vspaceUnmap(data)

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace
Unmap with shootdown and I-cache broadcast

steps.narrative: The mapping is removed and a TLB shootdown round evicts the cached translation on every core, so no stale entry can still reach the page.

scenarios.title: Two cores and thread migration
scenarios.summary: Each core schedules its own run queue. Moving a thread between cores is an explicit tcbSetAffinity syscall: a ready thread's run-queue entry moves to its new home core, but a thread running on a core its new affinity excludes cannot be moved.

steps.title: Initial state
steps.narrative: Core 0 runs w0 with w2 queued; core 1 runs w1 with w3 queued. Each core selects only from its own run queue.

steps.title: w0 → tcbSetAffinity(w3, core 0)

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: w3 is ready, not running, so it can move: the kernel sets its affinity and migrates its run-queue entry (and its scheduling context's replenishments) from core 1 to core 0, then signals core 0 to reschedule. w3 is never in two queues at once.

steps.title: w0 → tcbSetAffinity(w1, core 0) — refused

path.label: Resolve the capability in the caller's CSpace

steps.narrative: w1 is running on core 1 right now, and the new affinity excludes core 1. Pulling a running thread off another core mid-execution is refused with .threadOnDifferentCore; nothing changes on either core.

steps.title: core 1 timer — w1 charged
steps.narrative: Core 1's timer charges w1 independently of core 0. Its queue is now empty, so w1 keeps running when budget remains.
